title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: John James pushes local say on data centers amid Saline fights and primary votes.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. It's Sunday, August 2, and we're starting the day with the latest on these massive projects and how they're reshaping towns across the state.
Our big story today is U.S. Senate candidate John James telling The Detroit News he'd leave data-center siting and tax decisions up to local officials instead of state rules.
That stance lands right in the middle of active fights in places like Saline and Coldwater. Why does handing it to townships matter so much right now?
Because those communities are already dealing with proposals that could pull hundreds of megawatts, draw serious water, and change tax bases. James says locals know their needs best.
But what happens when one township says yes and the next one over gets hit with higher electric rates or noise complaints? We've seen that pattern before.
Exactly. Residents 30 minutes from some sites are already worried about grid strain if these campuses come online without new generation. The power has to come from somewhere.
And water use is another big one. These facilities need cooling. How many townships have already hit pause because of that?
Otsego just voted yesterday for a full 12-month ban on new proposals. That gives folks time to write rules on noise and infrastructure before anything big lands.
Genesee County also delayed an environmental vote this week. More time for public review on traffic, power, and industrial noise. It feels like a wave of local pushback.
At the same time, some places are rolling out the welcome mat. Mason County is bidding to host Michigan's official state data center, hoping for construction jobs and long-term revenue.

So the debate is really about who decides the trade-offs. James wants it at the township level. How does that square with candidates like El-Sayed who are out there blasting tax breaks and grid impacts?
El-Sayed held a rally at the Saline site on Friday to highlight those exact concerns. He argues big deals can raise rates for everyone nearby without enough oversight.
And voters get a say on Tuesday in the primary. Does James's position help or hurt him in counties already seeing these fights?

That's the open question. Supporters say it respects local control and avoids one-size-fits-all rules from Lansing. Critics worry it leaves smaller towns without enough leverage against big developers.
What about the history here? How long has this tension been building?
Proposals have accelerated with the AI boom. We've seen similar pauses and reviews in multiple counties this year as residents raise farmland loss, constant noise, and bill impacts.
Noise is real. In Dowagiac, neighbors are still litigating a high-pitched whine from the facility that runs day and night. That complaint is now shaping how Cass County handles the next round.

And yesterday Hyperscale Data announced a shift at its Dowagiac campus from Bitcoin mining to a 20-megawatt AI hosting contract under a 10-year deal. It could generate over a billion dollars, but the noise fight continues.
So even when the use changes, the community impacts stay the same. Power demand is still there.
Right. And a congressman is now calling for a federal review of Chinese robots at that same Michigan site, raising supply-chain and job questions.
That adds another layer. Local projects suddenly have national security angles too.
Verrus is pushing ahead on one Michigan project while its Salem plans stall. No exact site disclosed yet, but officials are already fielding questions on power and tax deals.
Coldwater residents got their first public look at plans on Friday. Same questions everywhere: how much power, how much water, what tax breaks?
Those are the stakes James is betting local officials can handle best. The primary on Tuesday will test whether voters agree.
And if more townships follow Otsego's lead with temporary bans, we could see a patchwork of rules instead of uniform state policy.
That's the bigger picture behind his statement. Now let's hit the other stories from this weekend.
Starting with Dowagiac. The 20-megawatt AI deal is a big shift for that site.
Yes, and residents are still dealing with the noise litigation even as the economic numbers look strong over the full contract term.
Genesee County postponed its environmental clearance vote. That buys extra weeks for people to review traffic and power impacts.
Otsego's one-year ban gives the community breathing room to shape protections before any big demands hit local infrastructure.
Mason County's pitch for the state data center puts a rural western Michigan spot in competition with bigger metro areas for jobs and revenue.
Coldwater's joint meeting on Friday let residents ask directly about power, water, and tax breaks on the table.
Verrus moving forward elsewhere while Salem stalls shows how fluid these site decisions can be.
El-Sayed's rally at Saline framed the local projects as central to the Democratic primary debate on tax breaks and grid strain.
And the congressman's call for review of equipment at the Hyperscale site adds federal scrutiny that could affect timelines.
Dowagiac noise complaints are already influencing how Cass County approaches future proposals to protect sleep and property values.
That's the quick hits for this morning. Now, what's on deck for listeners who want to get involved?
Tomorrow, August 3, the Delta County Planning Commission has a Data Center Subcommittee update and zoning ordinance discussion.
That's a chance for residents to weigh in on rules before anything moves forward there.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening. Stay informed on how these projects are shaping Michigan.

episode_title: Local Control Clash: James Backs Town Rules on Data Centers
